Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee:
Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony. My name is Amy Tague, a resident of Portland, and I'm here on behalf of HopeGateWay, a community of faith in Portland, Maine. The words of Micah 6:8 inspire our mission: to do justice, to love kindness, and to walk humbly with God. I am writing to vehemently oppose LD 233, LD 868, LD 1002, LD 1134, LD 1704, LD 1337, LD 1432, and LD 380. As a person of faith, parent, and social worker, I write to you with deep concern about these bills that seek to restrict access to sports teams, public restrooms, health care, and legal protections against discrimination based on gender identity.
My faith tells me we must protect the most vulnerable among us. Throughout his ministry, Jesus consistently stood with those whom religious and political authority marginalized, misunderstood, and mistreated. Right now, trans youth are one of the most vulnerable communities within this state and the country. These bills are incredibly harmful because they further marginalize an already marginalized group of students and adults who have the same right to a safe, supportive environment as their peers. To deny them the right to participate in their daily life based on who they are is unjust, unfair, and anti-Christian. And, frankly, it's not how we do things in Maine.
As someone with a personal connection to other states that have banned gender-affirming care and access to sports teams and public restrooms, I am, sadly, aware of the harmful impact of these bills. They upend the lives of adolescents, exploring different values, beliefs, and interests to form a sense of who they are and what they want in life. Here in Maine, we share a deep understanding of community and care for our neighbors, regardless of our differences in life experiences. We organize meal trains, community fundraisers, barter goods for services, swap produce, and trade gardening tips. Alongside our neighbors, we cheer for and encourage our student-athletes.
I implore you to stop these harmful bills from moving forward. As a person of faith and resident of Maine, I'm asking that you choose inclusion over exclusion and justice over discrimination. Let us be a kind community where all children-transgender children included- are seen, safe, and celebrated.
Thank you for the opportunity to share my perspective.

That's because In Maine, we don't exclude children for being different--we celebrate them. However, that is exactly what these bills are about - exclusion. I think about the many children-- much like my own, top students with talents and skills our state desperately needs--who are watching closely as we debate who deserves to participate fully. The message we send today will directly influence whether they choose to build their futures here in Maine. These young people and their allies are not residents Maine can afford to lose.
I was a decent athlete in school and have coached various youth sports, and I can tell you firsthand that the fears driving these bills simply don't match reality. I cannot count the number of times I've witnessed co-ed sports done successfully and safely. Female teams regularly scrimmage male teams without great risk of physical danger. Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee. Thank you for the opportunity to address the Committee.
My name is Aoife Dowd and I'm a resident of Portland. I'm here today to oppose the slew of bills targeting trans kids in our state. As a queer woman married to a trans man, I care very deeply about the trans community and wellbeing of trans kids.

Sexist behavior, sexual harassment, abuse from coaches, racism, poor facilities and funding, scrutiny of their bodies are all things much more likely to plague girls in sports. These laws only seek to magnify attention on girls and their bodies, putting them at elevated risk.

LD1002 endangers trans and queer kids and puts many of them in the position of choosing to live authentically, or "out" themselves to potentially unsupportive parents; an impossible decision with potentially dangerous consequences for the child.

10052461:
Ought Not to Pass - Testimony Joint Standing Committee on the Judiciary
Ariel Linet Portland, Maine May 8, 2025
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee,
Thank you for the opportunity to address the Committee. I submit this written testimony in opposition to eight bills before you today: LD 233, LD 868, LD 1002, LD 1134, LD 1704, LD 1337, LD 1432, and LD 380. These bills are cruel, harmful, and poor public policy; they are the opposite of what Mainers stand for, as I am sure you will see today by the number of people passionately urging you to vote Ought Not to Pass for all eight of the bills.
I am not transgender. However, many of the people I love are transgender, and the world is a better and brighter place with all of them in it, in the full depth and breadth of their identities. The world is a stunningly diverse place far beyond our comprehension or control. Or, as Shakespeare put it, "There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio,/Than are dreamt of in your philosophy." Trans people have always been here, they always will be here, and they have just as much of a right to exist and thrive and pursue their dreams as anyone else. This Legislature should not deny their humanity.
Trans people are not hurting or oppressing others in bathrooms or locker rooms. This is just not an actual problem that exists in the world, but rather a disingenuous right-wing boogeyman that is distracting us from the many legitimate problems we should be addressing. I am a cisgender woman and I have never felt unsafe around a trans person in a bathroom. However, I have (as have all of the women I know) felt unsafe around cisgender men in elevators, on sidewalks, and in various other public places. There are plenty of worthy organizations in Maine doing essential work to address toxic gender dynamics, and all of them stand against these bigoted bills.
I am the parent of a four-year-old, and there is one message I want to convey to my child above all others: that I will always love and support my child - gay, straight, trans, cis - it truly does not matter. I cannot imagine trying to force my child to inhabit an identity that feels wrong and harmful in order to win my love or acceptance. And it breaks my heart to think that we are doing that to any of our kids. We are all responsible to and for the next generation, and they deserve the very best we can give them. That includes voting Ought Not to Pass on LD 233, LD 868, LD 1002, LD 1134, LD 1704, LD 1337, LD 1432, and LD 380.
Thank you for your consideration and for your work on behalf of all Mainers.
10053909:
My name is Arnold Macdonald. I live in Freeport. I have testified here before as the Chair of the Business Law Section of the Maine State Bar Association and as the Chair of the Maine Justice Foundation. I have also been the President of the South Freeport Church, and coached Little League baseball for about ten years. My wife is retired after 30+ years as a public school teacher.
I am also the proud parent of a trans daughter. I was surprised when she "came out" to us 3 � years ago. At first I was a bit uncertain, and had to let go of dreams of a particular future with this son. I also worried that I missed things that could have let me be more helpful in her youth. I thought back to her changing nicknames, a brief but pronounced tic, trichotillomania (the irresistible urge to pull or break one's own hair) resulting in bald spots, and a time of malaise beginning in high school and getting worse until she transitioned 8-9 years after college. She did not seem fully comfortable in her own skin and was losing the confidence and leadership skills I saw when she was younger. Like any other parent here, nothing is more important to me than the happiness of my children and I am never fully happy unless mine are.
I can promise all of you that my daughter did not "choose" her gender to gain a competitive advantage at sports. I think that her experience in high school was not that different than mine or many others: feeling awkward, anxious, wanting desperately to fit in, not entirely sure how; only she had WAY more to overcome than I did.
It has been a great joy watching my daughter blossom and flourish since she has transitioned. She has regained confidence and leadership skills. Even as she is fundamentally the same person with the same values, I love some of her "feminine" changes as she and my wife shop together for clothes and jewelry and interact more as peers. The time she and I spend together, whether shopping or playing music or hiking in the woods, more open and honest and loving. She is equally a woman when wearing steel-toed boots and swinging a hammer, or erecting scaffolding and moving equipment at her job. She finds that she is happier doing everything in her life and closer to everyone she loves than she was before. She is more beautiful as a woman than she was handsome as a male.
I am not a biologist or neuroscientist and cannot talk about the science of gender. I suspect that very few of you can either. We all, however, know when our children are happy, and I know she is now.
My daughter does not go to public restrooms as a voyeur but rather as a person who wants to go peacefully without being threatened by hateful people. Pretty much the same as everyone else. She participates in online forums where trans women look for advice on coming out, and their overwhelming wisdom on bathroom use is that you should use the bathrooms most comfortable for you AND the other people in there. They care about others involved.
As a parent, former coach, and lifelong athlete I love the values of cooperation, teamwork, fair play, and competition sports teach. I believe the wide participation of American kids in sports

has a lot to do with our international leadership in business, the arts, and academia relative to other countries. Every American kid should have the opportunity to participate in sports and learn these skills.
Kids who dress and act and identify as girls should neither be singled out and excluded, nor forced to compete with boys. Kids and adults should be able to use the restrooms consistent with how they look and feel and act. Do you want kids who dress and look and act and are treated as boys going into girls' bathrooms? Kids who dress and look and act and are treated as girls using boys' bathrooms? That makes EVERYONE uncomfortable.
Excluding students draws attention and invites bullying and exclusion of kids who are already at risk.
I understand that Division I schools allow trans women with testosterone below a certain level to compete. The Olympics bar women born with vaginas from competing if their testosterone is above a certain level. Nobody uses the X and Y chromosome combinations we learned about in 9th grade science to determine gender, as there are too many variations and deviations for it to be useful.
Personally, I find the idea of hormonal testing of high school kids to qualify to participate in sports offensive and degrading. Even worse is the idea that students should have to pull down their pants in front of gender judges before participating in sports or using the bathroom of their choice. All students, not just identified trans girls, would be open to testing. Who would you want to invasively examine your kids?
I think that a big issue here is one of choice. Once the political right favored local choice and charter schools to offer kids a variety of options. My kids were in a wonderful elementary school in Freeport where you could choose between three programs with different approaches based on single classroom with one grade, moving rooms during the day and mixing kids of different ages, and degree of student input on subject matter. Portland has three different high schools with different approaches. Ideally families could choose between sports programs more focused on playing and developing everyone, or some could choose ones more focused on training kids to compete at a higher level. Even there, however, kids would face invasive testing and the possibility that kids gendered female at birth might fall within the 1 or 2 % with testosterone levels to compete in the Olympics or with trans girls whose testosterone is low enough to compete at all levels, or whose visible gender does not match their chromosomes.
Whether sports, books in libraries, or course content it seems that many people who favored local choice now want to force policy nationally and censor local control the instant they feel they have power.
I also caution against overreacting action in this political environment. I believe there is a popular image of trans women trying to gain unfair advantages and beat up on smaller, weaker children is a false one pushed by social media and the far right to fuel anti-trans fear and hatred.

This provides cover as leaders try, among other things, to remove all civil rights of trans people including protection from housing and employment discrimination, to fire them from military and other public jobs, and to house them in prisons other than those of their gender where they will be beaten and humiliated. We are too good to be part of that.
My daughter has suffered violence while riding the subway. I fear every day for the safety of my daughter and wish that she could walk the streets free from fear of harassment because of who she is.
My daughter with my wife and my nonbinary child with their band.

Sports was everything to me growing up- it was the escape I so desperately needed from my life. I was only used to playing on girls teams, having to wear a

Honestly, it was one of the best things to happen to me. I could finally compete with teammates that
allowed me to express and affirm who I really was. But more than that, it helped me feel like I belonged in my community, Like I was not an outsider, like I was excited to live. It helped shape who I am today.
Additionally, despite playing soccer on a boys team and being assigned female at birth- I was not

Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee,
Thank you for the opportunity to participate in the Committee's process today. My name is Ashley Schumacher. I am submitting this writing in opposition of the following bills before the committee today:
LD 233, An Act to Prohibit Biological Males from Participating in School Athletic Programs and Activities Designated for Females When State Funding Is Provided to the School LD 868, An Act to Ensure Equity and Safety in Athletics, Restrooms, Changing Rooms and Housing at Elementary, Secondary and Postsecondary Schools LD 1002, An Act to Protect Children's Identification by Requiring Public Schools to Use the Name and Gender Specified on a Child's Birth Certificate LD 1134, An Act to Prohibit Males from Participating in Female Sports or Using Female Facilities LD 1704, An Act to Prohibit a School Administrative Unit from Adopting a Policy That Allows a Student to Use a Restroom Designated for Use by the Opposite Sex
As someone with 17 years in the caring profession of nursing, a 2008 graduate of the University of Maine with a BS in Nursing and a BA in Women's Studies, and a nonbinary and queer individual with a family of my own, I have seen firsthand how the inclusion of transgender and gender expansive young people in our school communities has benefitted every Maine student. Being more accepting of marginalized groups harms no one and, in fact, betters us as a whole.

Because in part of this lack of representation and inclusion around me, I physically harmed myself as a teen, nearly ending my own life. That ought not sound like a threat to any members of our government, but a call to protect all of our state's youth. Our Maine transgender youth are not scapegoats to be used for political gain. They are real young people trying to navigate this world, who are as deserving of care, support, and legal protection as any other child in Maine.

Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee. Thank you for the opportunity to submit my testimony. My name is Lyn Bell. I'm a resident of Norway. I served my country and my community until my retirements as a Marine and a deputy sheriff. I have continued to serve locally as a teacher, and an elected official in Oxford County. I write as a representative of the First Universalist Church of Norway, and I am the parent of a transgender child. I am writing in opposition to the bills before the committee today, specifically LD 1134. My first experience with transgender students was while my family was living in Washington state and my own child came out as transgender. The schools were supportive, and we were thankful for the stability that provided our child. After moving to Maine, I began working as a substitute teacher, and I have been elated at the support and recognition my school system gives to their transgender students. For a kid who's struggling with feelings that aren't the same as the kids around them, the acceptance of the staff and students of their preferred name and gender inoculates them against the suicidal ideation and keeps them in school that plague transgender and non-binary individuals. Understand, it is not the condition of being transgender that causes the suicidal ideations - it is the societal response to them that causes it. Unfortunately, the prevailing ignorance in our society from the compassionless leaders who are unwilling to learn beyond middle school science models, imprints on parents of some of these students. This learned ignorance keeps parents from accepting and properly providing for their transgender children. For those children, the only acceptance they find is in the classroom. If you enact this proposal, you will do nothing to protect a child's identity. It will leave many of Maine's transgender students feeling as if they will never find acceptance of who they are, and that thinking will take them down a very dark road. If the authors and supporters of these bills wanted to protect children, they would do more to educate and assure the parents of transgender children, rather than turning those children into victims of societal ignorance. Thank you for the opportunity to share my perspective with the Committee. I urge you to vote "Ought not to Pass" on these bills. Thank you, Lyn Bell lynandheather@gmail.com

Avery Munns Auburn, Maine May 8, 2025
Dear Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee,
Thank you for the opportunity to address the Committee. My name is Avery Munns. I am a registered
voter in Auburn, and l am a teacher in the Lewiston Public Schools district. l am here in opposition
of the bill before the committee today.
My transition saved my life--l went from not being able to remember anything but a dark cloud
hovering over me to today where l feel free, happy, and at peace. The only regret l have is not starting my medical transition sooner. l often wonder how many years of suffering l could have alleviated if l had started my transition when l was an adolescent.
One reason l didn't start my medical transition sooner was due to misinformation about hormone replacement therapy (HRT). l thought that it might act like a magic potion that transformed me into a full-blown, hairy, bearded, massive adult man overnight. Afier listening to my reservations, my doctor recommended l start out on a very low dose of testosterone. At my three month checkup, not a single irreversible change had yet occurred. At that point, 1 could have quit HRT with no permanent
changes, but l was loving some of the small shifts l was seeing and decided to move up to a full dose. lt ended up being six months in total before my voice dropped in the slightest--one of the few
permanent changes of testosterone HRT. As my story shows, changes happen very gradually, and
there are very few irreversible changes of both testosterone and estrogen HRT. lf someone doesn't
like the changes that are occurring,'they will be able to talk with their doctor-a doctor who has sworn
the Hippocratic oath to "first, do no harm." Gender-affirming healthcare does not harm adolescents. lt is a slow process where the patient and doctor work together and monitor everything the entire
way.
Additionally, puberty blockers are entirely reversible. lf someone decides they don't want to be on
puberty blockers, they may stop and normal puberty will occur. 1 trust doctors and adolescents to be able to make these decisions for themselves and to be able to navigate the slow process of
gender-affirming healthcare together.
Thank you again for the opportunity to share my perspective with the Committee. l urge you to vote
"Ought not to Pass" on this bill. Thank you and have a great day.

Middle schoolers shared similar data, with 32.7% felt sad or hopeless, and 21.8% have seriously considered suicide. In both age ranges, 8% students had attempted suicide at least once. Bills that require teachers to call students by names make them uncomfortable, force them into going into bathrooms that might make them feel unsafe, and isolate them from their friends and teammates, undercut all the work we are meant to be doing as educators. ,

~

Dear Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary
Committee, Thank you for the opportunity to address the Committee. I am Caroline FreeSpirit, a resident of Standish, Maine. I am here as a citizen and resident of Maine. I am here to testify in
opposition to this bill.
The basic argument that supports allowing discrimination based on gender identity, indeed the foundation of all these arguments being presented today, is very straightforward, and pretends
to be based in science and common sense. In essence, the argument is that there are only two sexes, two genders, male and female, XY and XX chromosomes, and anyone who says
otherwise is wrong.

the premise is incorrect.
The documented science of the makeup of sex and gender is that 1.7% of the human population is, in fact, Intersex per Blackless et al. (2000). This means they have mixed presentations of external genitalia and internal chromosomal makeup. The argument that there
are only two sexes, only two genders, male and female, only XY and XX chromosomes is wrong. I am not even addressing transgender individuals when I make this assertion. There are men with XX genes, and women with XY genes, and people with mixed presentations. I am asking that you do not build a structure of discrimination based on this flimsy premise. This
lie that there are only two sexes is also used to support all the transgender phobic nonsense
that we are witnessing today. Please vote against this bill.

To: Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Senate Judiciary Committee
From: Carrie Sherman, Maine resident, Kittery Point, Maine 03905
Re: Bills regarding Trans Students in Maine schools, hearing to be held May 8
Thank you for the opportunity to submit written testimony for the committee to consider. I am here in opposition of the bills before the committee today.
As an educator at a nearby community college, many of my students were allies of or part of the transgender community. Talking with them and reading their essays was very enlightening for me. I developed great compassion and respect for them. As well, at my church, transgender people have the courage and feel accepted to participate actively in our services. I am deeply grateful to them for sharing their stories. As a result, I have become more comfortable and skilled as a teacher in regards to the transgender community. I was also able to model that behavior for my students. It didn't take long to achieve this, and it wasn't hard.
For me, it comes down to this: the reality of being transgender has been around since time began. We are merely accepting this reality. Many cultures always have.
A 2018 Scientific American article examined recent research regarding DNA and the ongoing development of sexual orientation and gender identity as a person matures. Author Claire Ainsworth, quotes Eric Villain, a clinician and the director of the Center for Gender-Based Biology at the University of California, Los Angeles. He notes: "It has been, in a sense, a philosophical change in our way of looking at sex; that it's a balance. It's more of a systemsbiology view of the world of sex."
Let's not burden our educational communities with divisive, punitive laws that create fingerpointing and shame. Girls are already unduly vulnerable to stereotypes about their bodies given the ongoing blast of social media. Adolescents in general are having a rough time trying to catch up educationally after the pandemic.
What we want in our schools are strong, supportive communities. We want to teach our students well and give them critical skills to succeed as adults. Students learn best when they are treated fairly and respectfully.
One of my last years of teaching, the women's basketball team had a really great season. Their magnificent playing totally galvanized the school. Everyone showed up at their games and the cool hoodies emblazoned with the school's mascot just about sold out. Everyone agreed, the team's success was all about teamwork.

As for differences, with the support of strong communities, these students work it out. They're good kids.
Thank you for the opportunity to share my perspective with the Committee. I urge you to vote "Ought not to pass" on these bills. Thank you.

Hello Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee,

For 16 years, I raised my little boy and cherished the relationship we had. When my now daughter was 16, she said to me, "Papa, I feel more like a girl inside than a boy, and I'm afraid it's going to change our relationship." I responded, "first, we are connected forever and in many ways that will never change. Second, part of the joy of being your parent is to see how you are becoming and this is part of that."
Over the past three years, I have seen my daughter becoming a young woman and have been fortunate to witness and be part of that deep truth. At the same time, it is hard to see some people driven by fear of what they do not understand, use trans people as political pawns, and try to erase the beauty and truth of them as human beings and their experience. I have also experienced my daughter in substantial pain when she feels like people do not see her as a real woman, and that breaks my heart.
Some people see "problems" with transpeople. LD 1134 is an example. To address the issue of trans girls participating in sports and using facilities with the gender community to which they belong, LD 1134 pursues a misguided and mistaken solution that blames and hurts trans people by excluding and erasing them. The problem is not with trans people! The problem lies within our society that, based on fear of difference, seeks to enforce a ridged, exclusionary, and simplistic world. This world is in complete contradiction to the entire concept of human rights, to The Maine Human Rights Act, and to An Act To Clarify Various Provisions of the Maine Human Rights Act. This history, and these institutions and laws are predicated on the fundamental

inherent value of all humans, not just certain humans. This fundamental right must be protected both because of the inherent value of all humans, and because our world is poorer when we exclude people.
More productive actions with better outcomes would include looking at ourselves, owning our biases and our fear, and working to figure out how to include humans in their many expressions of humanity. It is easy to find communities around the world that include trans people. Examples include communities in North America, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Africa, and the Pacific. They have done it. Are we less capable than them?
LD 1134, put forth by some legislators, is attempting to codify complicity with the exclusion, erasing and violence done to trans people. It effectively says, "we do not accept the way you are expressing your woman-ness, your humanity." Coming from state leaders and a legislative body, LD 1134 supports the underlying logic that motivates people to do harm to trans people.
Thank you for the opportunity to share my perspective with the Committee. I urge you to vote "Ought not to Pass" on LD 1134. Thank you.
Sincerely,
Christopher Swartley

10052468:
LD 1134 An Act to Prohibit Males from Participating in Female Sports or Using Female Facilities Sen. Sue Bernard of Aroostook
Testimony to Maine Legislature Judiciary Committee Christine Hart, M.A. International Human Rights South Portland, Maine 04106
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on the Judiciary,
Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony to express my strong opposition to LD 1134, An Act to Prohibit Males from Participating in Female Sports or Using Female Facilities.
I am a Mainer, a human rights professional, and the family member and friend of a number of trans individuals, who I love and respect dearly. This bill deliberately and cruelly targets the most basic humanity, worth, and dignity of trans individuals and, what's worse, takes aim at children.
This bill is not about protecting fairness or safety--it is about targeting a small, vulnerable group of young people in Maine for political gain. By seeking to ban transgender girls from school sports and bar them from using facilities aligned with their gender identity, LD 1134 singles out transgender students for exclusion and public scrutiny. When we legislate against a handful of young people who are already navigating a hostile and often misunderstood world, we are not crafting policy--we are engaging in state-sanctioned bullying.
There are reportedly only two publicly known transgender girls currently participating in school athletics in Maine. Yet this legislation would upend statewide policy and put all schools at risk of violating civil rights law just to exclude these few students. That is not governance; that is a political ploy that comes at the direct expense of children's mental health and basic dignity.
Research consistently shows that transgender youth in sports benefit significantly from participation. According to a 2022 study published by the American Journal of Public Health, transgender athletes who participate in school sports report higher levels of mental well-being, lower rates of depression, and improved social integration. Participation in sports not only improves physical health but also boosts self-esteem and provides a sense of community and belonging.
A 2021 study from the Journal of Sport and Social Issues found that transgender girls who are allowed to compete in sports that align with their gender identity experience significantly improved mental health outcomes compared to their peers who are excluded. These benefits are especially important for transgender youth, who face disproportionately high rates of mental health challenges. According to research conducted by The Trevor Project in 2024, anti-transgender laws cause up to a 72% increase in suicide attempts among transgender and nonbinary youth. Transgender youth who are able to express their gender identity in supportive spaces, including sports, report significantly lower rates of depression and suicidality.

The 2021 GLSEN National School Climate Survey also reported that 60% of transgender students avoid gym class due to feelings of discomfort and discrimination, a trend that worsens when students are barred from participating in activities consistent with their gender identity. Excluding transgender girls from school sports and facilities would further isolate them and drive up absenteeism and disengagement.
This bill also flies in the face of established legal precedent. In Doe v. Regional School Unit 26 (2014), the Maine Supreme Judicial Court affirmed a transgender student's right to use the bathroom consistent with her gender identity under the Maine Human Rights Act. LD 1134 would directly contradict this ruling and expose Maine schools to legal liability and public backlash.
Instead of ensuring equity or safety, LD 1134 encourages stigma, division, and harm. It sends a chilling message to transgender youth across the state: that their identity is up for public debate, and that their basic human rights can be stripped away through political theater. Maine should be a place where all students are treated with respect and protected from discrimination--not where our laws are weaponized against those with the least power.
Thank you for your service and consideration of this issue. I respectfully urge the Committee in the strongest terms to vote "Ought Not to Pass" on LD 1134. Protecting children means all children--including transgender children.

Dear Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee,
My name is Claire Horne and I am a resident of Appleton, Maine. I am writing in opposition of the bills before you today: LD 233; LD 868; LD 1002; LD 1134; and LD 1704.
I went to public school in Maine from Kindergarten through high school. In that time, I participated in many athletic programs. I started playing basketball with my older sister before I was even old enough to be on a team, I eventually joined teams at the YMCA for elementary school aged kids, and then played on a school team throughout my middle school years. I also played soccer and softball in middle school, then soccer, Nordic skiing, and lacrosse in high school. I competed on and against many different teams. My soccer team throughout middle school was co-ed and we played lots of other co-ed teams around the region. I really liked being part of a co-ed team because we were appreciative of each others' skills and specialties rather than judged by our gender or age. In high school I really liked being on a Nordic ski team that trained together, people of all genders. Bigger, supportive teams meant I enjoyed being at practice and I had more capacity to be challenged to perform my personal best. In these experiences on teams with people of all genders, I never felt like I was put at a disadvantage because I was matched against someone of a different gender. I especially never experienced being put at a disadvantage by any trans girls that were playing against me. This harmful myth that athletics are somehow unfair if everyone is allowed to participate harms everyone. Athletics can and should be a space of inclusion.
As a student athlete, I spent a lot of time in bathrooms and locker rooms. My experience was that everyone was respectful of other people's privacy because that's how you wanted to be treated. We are seeing in examples across the country now that bathroom bans and other policies restricting access to facilities based on gender or sex creates increased speculation and policing for everyone. It creates a subjective standard for who "looks like a girl" that is harmful to put people through at any age. My experience as a young person, particularly as a young girl, was feeling unwanted scrutiny on my body from adult administrators and teachers at school who would police what I was allowed to wear at school and make shaming comments if they thought I should be covering up more. I never felt this scrutiny from teammates or peers that I shared a changing room or restroom with. These bills invite increased

scrutiny into how young people's bodies look. Policing the appearance of children and minors is completely inappropriate and creates a culture of fear that disrupts the entire school and athletic experience. Enforcing who can use what facilities based on a birth certificate is dehumanizing to the child that is trying to get a basic human need met. A child or young person being policed by an adult is much more likely to be harmed than to do anyone else any harm. This is how bathroom and athletics bans harm everyone - they force children to have anxiety about how they look and fear of an adult telling them they have to do something against their consent that doesn't align with their identity. Why would we willingly inflict this upon our youth?
Further, it is completely unnecessary to require that children be called by the name on their birth certificate in school. I know many people who go by different names to what is on their birth certificate for lots of different reasons. Some have nicknames they prefer, others go by a middle name or their last name, some want to use a name that they like that feels like it matches them better. It doesn't harm anyone to call someone by the name they want, but it does cause harm to force teachers and administrators to call students names that feel wrong to them. The same goes for misgendering students and forcing them to use restrooms that don't align with who they are. None of these bills respect the autonomy of students.
My experience has been that school athletics can help us to build connections with our peers, move our bodies, and learn new skills. This cannot happen if children and young people are being policed or scrutinized for how they look, what bathroom they use, what their name is, or any other attributes. It is vital that this harmful legislation is opposed so that all children and young people can have inclusive and welcoming experiences at school and athletics without repressive policies.
Thank you for your time and attention. I strongly urge you to vote "Ought not to Pass" on all aforementioned bills to protect students, athletes, and all young people from harmful scrutiny.
Sincerely, Claire Horne Appleton, Maine

Chairperson and Members of the Judiciary Committee,
My name is Colleen Brown. I am a parent of two daughters, a grandparent, and an educator. I am writing today in support of LD 233, LD 868, LD 1002, LD 1134, LD 1704, LD 1337, and LD 1432. These bills address a growing concern that I, and many others, share regarding the erosion of sex-based protections and the need to restore clarity, fairness, and safety in law and policy.
This is not about exclusion. It is about fairness, privacy, and protecting the hard-won rights of women and girls. Title IX was created to ensure that females had equal access to athletic opportunities. Allowing biological males, who possess undeniable physiological advantages, to compete in female sports undermines those protections and puts girls at a disadvantage both on the field and in life.
As an educator, I have seen how opportunities in sports build confidence, leadership skills, and academic access through scholarships. As a parent and grandparent, I am deeply concerned about the consequences of allowing biological males into female-designated bathrooms and locker rooms. These are spaces meant for privacy and safety, especially for young girls. No girl should be told that her discomfort in such spaces is irrelevant.
This issue extends beyond schools and into institutions like prisons and shelters. We are already seeing biological males identifying as female being placed in women's prisons and shelters, creating very real safety risks. In these settings, women cannot simply walk away, and the state has a duty to protect them.
I believe in treating all people with dignity and respect. That does not mean ignoring biological facts or removing safeguards for women and girls. These rights were established long before gender identity became a widely recognized concept. That reinforces a simple truth: sex, not self-perception, was and remains the legal foundation for these protections.
What message are we sending to our daughters when we say fairness no longer matters, or that their safety is secondary to ideological trends? This is not progress. It is a step backward.
I urge the committee to vote in favor of these bills and reaffirm the value of sex-based distinctions in law and policy. Maine has the opportunity to lead with clarity and courage.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Respectfully, Colleen Brown Whiting, Maine Parent, Grandparent, Educator

Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee:
My name is Danny Chin of Bath, ME and I am writing on May 7th in advance of the May 8th public hearing on a variety of anti-trans bills. I am grateful for the opportunity to offer written testimony to the Committee and to lend my voice in support of trans, non-binary, and other gender expansive Mainers. I am therefore writing in opposition to the bills before the committee on May 8th.
As a former educator and Gender-Sexuality Alliance (GSA) leader, I have first hand experience supporting trans and queer students as they navigate their school environments. These students are not a threat, but rather simply seek to exist and participate in school life. Many of their peers face few to no obstacles, and for trans and queer students, they are deserving of this same ease. By excluding these students from sports teams, bathrooms, and other facilities, this legislation seeks to exclude them from everyday life, deny them basic rights and privileges, and bar their full participation in society.
These bills use the language of safety and protection, but their passage will ultimately harm students, including those who are not trans. The vague language in these bills empowers individuals to scrutinize and police others' gender, gender identity, and gender expression.  Everyone suffers in a hostile, distrusting climate such as this. Furthermore, individuals can weaponize this paranoia to advance their own agenda. For example, without any proof or authority, a player on an opposing team can accuse another player of being trans simply because they look, act, or play a certain way. Unfortunately, we've seen this type of behavior even at the Olympic level, where unfounded accusations have sought to derail athletes' participation in sports that they love and to which they dedicate their lives. These baseless accusations can be used to interrupt competitive games, distract teams and athletes, and/or provide undeserved advantages. Beyond these reasons, we also lack the avenues to "prove" gender identity. If individuals must prove their gender, what non-invasive and private means are available for them to do so?
This legislation seeks to solve a problem that does not exist. Sports leagues, schools, and athletic associations already have rules for participation. Instead, we should be focusing on making schools inclusive environments where students can learn and grow without fear.
I appreciate this opportunity to share my perspective with the Committee. I urge you to vote "Ought not to Pass" on these bills. Thank you for your consideration.

10051949:
LD 1134: An Act to Prohibit Males from Participating in Female Sports or Using Female Facilities
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, Members of the Judiciary Committee, I am David Souers. living in Friendship, Maine. I am retired after a long career with my own firm practicing healthcare architecture designing clinics, hospitals, psychiatric facilities and specialty centers for women's health, maternity, surgery, cancer, dialysis and dentistry. My wife, Linda Souers joins me in this testimony. Linda is a retired art teacher, business manager and not-for-profit community board member. Linda and I are parents of three adult women, all of whom played sports from grade school through highschool. All three have careers in health and healthcare.
We are testifying in opposition to LD 1134 for the reasons, which we explain below. We also are in opposition to LD 233, LD 868, LD 1002, LD 1337, LD 1432, LD 380, LD 1134 and LD 1704 for all the reasons here and our other testimonies on these bills. But first, how do these proposed bills comply with the 2005 amendment to the MHRA which expanded the definition of "sexual orientation" to include "gender identity" and expression, which marked a significant step in ensuring equal treatment under the law?
1. This bill would ban any schools receiving state funding from allowing transgender girls to participate in school sports. Additionally, it would ban trans girls from using school facilities "designated for use solely by females." The bill is vague, and the meaning of "facilities" is unclear-this could potentially include a bathroom ban, taking us back more than a decade to debate an issue that has long been settled.
2. This bill fails to address any of the questions and issues that we have brought up in all the other transgender bills.
Rather than write bills without any scientific, medical or psychological expertise to support them, we advocate that LD 233, 868, 1002, 1337, 1432, 380, 1134, and 1704 all ought not to pass. And, that the legislature establish a study involving representatives from the state's public education groups including effective legal advice on gender law, administrators, classroom teachers, gym & sports coaches, school nurses along with professionals in the area of gender, adolescent and young adult medicine and psychology with experience in transgender study and care.
Thank you for your attention.
David & Linda Souers Friendship, ME

194105:
May 8, 2025, Augusta, Maine Public Testimony before the Judiciary
Committee of the Maine State Legislature, by David A. Weeda, a U.S.
citizen, residing in Bucksport, Maine.
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee. Thank you for the opportunity to address the
Committee.
My name is David A. Weeda, and I have been a resident citizen of Bucksport,
Maine, since October of 2003. I am here today to speak in firm opposition to
all 8 bills this Committee is looking at today; LD 233, LD 868, LD 1002, LD 1134, and LD 1704 -- in your 9:30 a.m. session, LD 1337 and LD 1432 -- in your 1 p.m. session, And LD 380 -- in your 3 p.m. session.
I am an openly gay cis gendered man, and at age 66, am able to reflect on over 45 years of advocacy and engaged public activism for the LGBTQIA+
community.
I have witnessed many gains and losses over those years, and I am no
stranger to the community-jubilation that comes with a legislative or electoral victory, or the heartbreaking sadness and community trauma which accompany the defeats.
An integral part of our shared humanity is the notion that we all crave a sense
of belonging as well as a feeling of being "seen" in our authentic identity.
Young people, in particular, need to feel safe and nurtured as they become
aware of their identity and how they might fit into our world as they mature.
Homophobia and transphobia harm us all. LGBTQIA+ people are real. We
have always been authentic members of our diverse human family, and any
legislation which seeks to deny our existence or full participation in our culture is unwarranted and cruel. Trans people are authentically fulfilling their personal destinies, and deserve every opportunity to participate in our
culture as they express their authentic gender-identity.

Our public schools have a particularly important role to play in a process which should allow all young people to joyfully and confidently embrace their identities. Relevant resources which provide authentic, honest support
should be available for any student who seeks them out. The notion of
prohibiting authentic acknowledgment and honest conversation around
human sexuality, our diversity in gender expression and sexual orientation, is
unhealthy, dishonest and divisive.
The goal of my advocacy and activism for the LGBTQlA+ community has
always been to make life safer, happier and more fulfilling for the next generation. The eight bills in front of your Committee today are meanspirited, and seek to further marginalize and harm our vulnerable transgender members of our human family.
Thank you.

Dawn Nuding, LCPC, ATR Lamoine Maine May 8, 2025
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee,
Thank you for the opportunity to address the Committee. My name is Dawn Nuding. I'm a resident of Lamoine and I am submitting testimony in opposition of all of the bills before the committee today.
Thank you for the opportunity to address the Committee. My name is Dawn Nuding. I'm a resident of Lamoine and I am submitting testimony in opposition of all of the anti-trans bills before the committee today.
For the past thirteen years I have worked in private practice as an Art Therapist and Licensed Clinical Professional Counselor, primarily with school aged youth and families. My caseload has included many people who are transgender and who identify as, non-binary and gender fluid. As a professional in the field, I know that the mental health of marginalized communities is statistically more at risk for higher rates of depression, anxiety and suicidal thinking, and I have certainly seen evidence of that in the clients I work with. I have also seen how affirming spaces, inclusion in community activities like sports and access to safe, affirming healthcare can increase resiliency exponentially. This resiliency is what strengthens the mental wellness of all populations. As part of our community, trans people deserve access to those basic resources. We have many essential safeguards to protect human rights in our state and our country including constitutional guarantees of equal protection and Title IX. Undoing or undermining those safeguards with bills like those before you today would be a step backwards in the fundamental rights of our state. I particularly worry that these bills suggest they are improving the protection of vulnerable populations like children and female athletes, when they are actually exploiting these populations to promote discriminatory and bigoted political views.
Trans people exist, and are undeniably part of our community. Banning access to resources or limiting the rights and protections of anyone in our community will cause widespread harm to the entire population. Our goal should be to move forward as a state, rather than backward. Vote against these bills to protect all citizens of Maine. Thank you for your consideration.
Dawn Nuding

Dear Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee;
My name is Dawn Walls. I am from the town of Unity. I am testifying in opposition to the bills before the committee today. (LDs 233, 868, 1002, 1134, and 1704). I strongly oppose these bills for the following reasons:
All of the bills being put forth today could accurately be called trans bans. They come in slightly differing forms, but that is what they all seek to do: ban trans students and trans people from participating equally and fully in our communities - their communities.
I find it a particular insult that some of these bills are proposed as "protecting women and girls". As a woman, I do not feel safer knowing that trans women are being oppressed. In fact, it is far more likely for a trans woman to be the victim of violence than to commit violence against anyone. As a woman, I have never felt threatened by any trans person. As a woman, I do feel threatened when legislations are proposed that seek to remove the equal protections and human rights of any of our citizens. I care about the rights of all women and girls, which also means trans women and girls. Trans rights are human rights.

What is under my skirt is no one's business. What is in my pants is no one's business.

To: Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn and Distinguished Members of the Judiciary Committee
My name is Debra Susi. I am a 38-year educator, the 2022 Somerset County Teacher of the Year and semifinalist for the 2023 Maine State Teacher of the Year. LD 1134: An Act to Prohibit Males from Participating in Female Sports or Using Female Facilities. Over nearly four decades, I've taught and supported thousands of students. I can say with confidence that nothing is more essential to student success than feeling safe, seen, and respected in school. This bill undermines that by targeting transgender and gender-diverse students--some of the most vulnerable youth in our care.
Legislating which restrooms students can use based on their sex assigned at birth not only disregards established best practices in education and child development, it sends a harmful message: that transgender students are not worthy of the same dignity and respect as their peers.

Denying individuals access to school sports and facilities consistent with their gender identity is not only unjust--it is unlawful.
Participation in athletics and access to facilities are vital parts of the school experience. They foster physical and mental well-being, teamwork, self-confidence, and belonging. When we exclude transgender students, we tell them they don't belong in our schools. That message is not only cruel--it puts lives at risk. Transgender youth already experience disproportionately high rates of depression, anxiety, and suicide, often driven by rejection and social isolation. I have worked directly with transgender students. I have seen them thrive when they are affirmed--and suffer deeply when they are not. Denying them access to facilities that match their identity is not about privacy or safety. It's about exclusion, plain and simple. This is not a hypothetical issue. These are real children. Real families. Real consequences.
Please, don't force schools and educators to turn their backs on students who need our support. Reject this bill, and choose compassion, inclusion, and evidence over fear.
Thank you for your time and your service.
I respectfully urge you to vote no on this bill. Thank you.

facilities that match their identity, and have their names and pronouns respected and affirmed. These are not privileges; they are fundamental aspects of dignity and well-being.
Rather than addressing genuine issues, these bills create problems where none exist. In a time
when we should be focusing on policies that uplift and support all young people, these bills
divert attention and resources toward legislating exclusion. They do not address pressing issues but instead perpetuate harm against a marginalized group. Rejecting these bills is not only a moral imperative but also a necessary step toward fostering a more inclusive and compassionate Maine.
Every day we partner with adults across the state and ask them to trust Maine youth, to invest in Maine youth. Today many of us here are asking you to do the same. l ask that you invest in the
safety, well-being, and sense of belonging for all Maine youth by rejecting these bills and any
similar efforts in the future.
Thank you for the opportunity to share my perspective with the Committee. I urge you to
vote for Maine trans youth and vote "Ought Not to Pass" on these bills. Thank you!

The intersection of the Maine Human Rights Act (MHRA) and Title IX presents a

Leading for equity, excellence and opportunity for all Maine Students

complex legal landscape for Maine school districts, particularly concerning the inclusion of transgender students in educational programs and activities. The MHRA prohibits discrimination in education based on gender identity, ensuring that individuals are not denied access to educational opportunities due to their gender identity. This state law mandates that public schools in Maine provide equal access and treatment to all students, including transgender individuals.
However, Title IX, a federal law that prohibits discrimination on the basis of sex in education programs or activities receiving federal financial assistance, has a conflicting"interpretation"at the federal level. It is important to point out that nowhere in Title IX does it speak specifically to or about transgender athletes.It strictly prohibits discrimination on the basis of sex. The current federal interpretation of Title IX, particularly concerning transgender students, has resulted in enforcement actions and federal investigations against Maine's policies that allow transgender students to participate in sports and use facilities consistent with their gender identity.
Maine's adherence to the MHRA, which includes gender identity as a protected class, conflicts with the federal interpretation of Title IX. This discrepancy places school districts in a challenging position, balancing state obligations to protect students from discrimination with federal requirements that may mandate exclusionary practices.
We understand that these issues are deeply important, and each community may have varying viewpoints. Our focus remains on ensuring that schools are inclusive and welcoming for all students, while balancing the legal and ethical responsibilities that come with these complex matters. We are committed to respecting both state laws and the realities of federal mandates while striving to support every student in an environment that fosters their growth and success.

Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee. Thank you for the opportunity to address the Committee and share my perspective. My name is Eleanor Schuttenberg, and I am a resident of Bangor. I am writing in opposition of LD1134. I am a PhD candidate in clinical psychology, specializing in working with children. As a part of this training, I work with children and adolescents who feel depressed, who feel anxious, and many of whom struggle with suicidal thoughts. Many of the youth I work with identify as transgender, non-binary, gender fluid, or are in the process of figuring out their own gender identity. While I have seen considerable joy from these youth, I have sat with youth as they have cried because they feel rejected, I have watched them avoid school because they feel as though there is no place for them, and I have witnessed them feel crushed by the laws and politics of our country telling them that they shouldn't exist. Children as young as nine years old have told me that if they cannot be who they are, if they cannot be the gender they know themselves as, that their only option is suicide. In those moments, as their therapist, I am there for them. I create a safe space for them in my office where they know they have rights, dignity, autonomy, and respect. But when these transgender youth leave my office, they feel the rest of the world trying to punish and erase them. I fear for them as they leave, but I take solace knowing that despite living in a country that stigmatizes them, Maine currently supports their rights.
As a PhD candidate, much of my life is spent reading scientific literature. I spend my time reading studies to try to be the most informed scientist, the best therapist, and the best advocate I can be for the children who walk into my office. And what the science tells us is what we already know: transgender and gender diverse people exist. Transgender people are not harmful. There is no evidence that allowing transgender youth to play on their gender-aligned sports teams hurts anyone. There is no evidence allowing children to use the restroom that aligns with their gender identity puts anyone in danger. There is no evidence that allowing a child to use their chosen name is harmful to anyone. Elite athletes can still get benefits of sport with transgender people around them. The bathrooms in Maine are safe when everyone is able to use them.
Transgender people, and transgender youth specifically, are acutely harmed by anti-trans legislation. Anti-transgender legislation can increase suicide attempts by up to 72%. One transgender person I worked with described that these anti-trans laws feel like "water on a stone" - one drop doesn't look like a lot, but over time they erode a person's sense of wellbeing and safety. Gender-affirming legislation and care saves the lives of children, adolescents, and adults. Our government has a responsibility to help remind people- all people- that they are safe from discrimination. Thank you for the opportunity to share my perspective with the Committee. I urge you to vote "Ought not to Pass" on LD1134. Thank you for your time.

Testimony - May 8th

My name is Eli Bundy, and I am a 20-year-old living in Brunswick, Maine and originally from South Carolina. I am thankful for the opportunity to speak today, but I wish that I did not have to. I am a trans person, a full time student, and I work to bring community together, both on my
school's campus and in the broader Brunswick area. I would rather be studying for exams right
now, but instead, I am speaking here today in strong opposition to all anti-trans bills before the

committee.

I

I fought anti-trans legislation in the South Carolina Legislature for four years as a high school
student, and I know how harmful anti-trans bills can be; for trans young people, for trans adults, for athletes, and for women, both cis and trans, whose bodies are more heavily policed and controlled when anti-trans policies are in place. After all, anti-trans legislation is ultimately about
the ability of the state to control the bodies of its people without their consent, and this sets a
dangerous precedent for the erosion of all of our rights.

Anti-trans legislation makes me feel small. It makes me feel like the elected officials meant to be
making decisions on behalf of their constituents only care about winning political points by harassing trans kids because they can, because trans kids, and trans people in general, are a
small minority without a loud political or financial voice. I am tired of asking politicians elected to serve the public to treat me as a human, to allow me the same rights and privileges that should
be guaranteed to all people in this country: to have healthcare, to be educated in an inclusive space, to engage in meaningful community and connection with people both alike and different
from us.

I was involved in youth sports throughout my childhood and adolescence, and I got to learn
about the importance of collaboration, of working through conflict, of persevering to solve hard
problems by being on sports teams. I changed clothes for PE in an actual closet (no joke) to avoid being lumped in with the girls or being ostracized by the guys. I was incredibly lucky to
have a supportive family, good health insurance, a great high school, and yet I struggled with
the feeling that I was completely unwelcome in the city and state in which I lived. I moved to
Maine, in part, to escape this feeling, but I have since learned that this hatred of and apathy
towards trans people is not unique to the south, but permeates every corner of this country.

However, this need not be the case. Trans people show the world that you do not need to accept the role you are given, that there are beautiful and expansive futures to be found in self-becoming, in community that is found through shared experience and struggle. Trans people will continue to exist everywhere no matter what laws are passed, but harassing and
targeting trans people for political points is dehumanizing and cruel.

I urge you to leave trans people alone and oppose these bigoted and harmful bills. Thank you
for your time.

Detailed Discussion of Why Women's Sports Legislation is Constitutional:
The Equal Protection Clause to the Fourteenth Amendment "command[s] that no State deny the equal protection of the laws to any person within its jurisdiction." Reed v. Reed, 404 U.S. 71, 74 (1971). But the Supreme Court "has consistently recognized that the Fourteenth Amendment does not deny to States the power to treat different classes of persons in different ways." Id. at 75 (emphasis added). And sex-based classifications are constitutional where
they "realistically reflect[ ] the fact that the sexes are not similarly situated in certain circumstances." Clark, 695 F.2d at 1129. Specifically, the Supreme Court recognizes that "[p] hysical" and "`[i]nherent differences' between
men and women" exist and that those differences are "enduring." United States v. Virginia, 518 U.S. 515, 533
(1996). So once the state demonstrates that a sex-based classification based on those differences (1) "serve[s] important governmental objectives," and (2) is "substantially related to achievement of those objectives," Craig v. Boren, 429 U.S. 190, 197 (1976), the state has carried its "burden of showing an exceedingly persuasivejustification
for [the] classification," Mississippi University for Women v. Hogan, 458 U.S. 718, 724 (1982) (cleaned up).
Based on this, federal courts have held that "redressing past discrimination against women in athletics and
promoting equality of athletic opportunity between the sexes" is a "legitimate and important govemmental interest." Clark, 695 F.2d at 1131.
In Clark, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reviewed an appeal brought by male high school athletes
who had been kept off the girls' volleyball teams despite the boys' prior success on national championship teams. Id. at 1127. The schools did not have boys' volleyball teams. Id. And a policy "preclude[d] boys from playing on [the] girls' teams." Id. The boys sued, arguing that "precluding [them] from playing on girls' interscholastic
volleyball teams . . . violate[d] the equal protection clause." Id.

The Court asked "whether the exclusion of boys is substantially related to [that] interest," or "whether any real differences exist between boys and girls which justify the exclusion," meaning "differences which would prevent realization of the goal if the exclusion were not allowed." Id. The Court found that there are. "[D]ue to average physiological differences, males would displace females to a substantial extent if they were allowed to compete for positions on the volleyball team." Id The parties had stipulated that, "[g]enerally, high school males are taller, can jump higher and are stronger than high school females." Ia.' at 1127. This lefi "no question . . . that boys [would] on average be potentially better volleyball players than girls." Id. (emphasis added). Accord Petrie, 394 N.E.2d at 863 ("Both because of past disparity of opportunity and because of innate differences, boys and girls are not similarly situated as they enter into most
athletic endeavors.").
Under intermediate scrutiny, this was enough. The Supreme Court has repeatedly allowed recognition ot"these average real differences between the sexes." Id. at 1131. And because the challenged policy "simply recogniz[ed] the
physiological fact that males would have an undue advantage competing against women for positions on the
volleyball team," there was "clearly a substantial relationship between the exclusion of males from the team and the goal of redressing past discrimination and providing equal opportunities for women." Id.

LD 1337, An Act to Amend the Maine Human Rights Act Regarding Female Athletes and Safety in Women's Shelters
May 8, 2025

Senator Camey, Representative Kuhn, and my esteemed colleagues of the Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary: I am Elizabeth Caruso and I have the honor of representing the people
of House District 72, which includes 33 municipalities in Somerset County. I am pleased to present to you LD 1337, "An Act to Amend the Maine Human Rights Act Regarding Female
Athletes and Safety in Women's Shelters."
Let me begin with a little bit of history. Before Title IX even existed, a young woman who was a volunteer attorney for the American Civil Liberties Union was a staunch advocate for women's
rights and defended the 14"` Amendment's equal protection clause. A feminist, this woman was
the architect of the legal fight for women's rights in the 1970s.

She defined what it was to be woman and fought for the rights that women and girls enjoy today. When she began her legal crusade, women by law were treated differently from men. Hundreds of state and federal laws restricted what women could do, barring them from jobs,
rights and even from jury service.

She would see the landmark federal Education Amendments of 1972, what we call Title IX, and would defend those rights until her death. And she once said, "I pray that I may be all that [my mother] would have been had she lived in an age when women could aspire and achieve and daughters are cherished as much as sons."

Her name was Ruth Bader Ginsberg.

193753:
Erica A. Boissonneault, Gorham Maine, May 8dl 2025
Senator Camey, Representative K.uhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee. Thank you for the opportunity to address you today. My name is Erica Boissonneault and I am a resident of Gorham Maine. I am hear to testify agamst proposed bill ME LD1432 An Act to Remove Consideration of Gender Identity from the Mame Human Rights Act.
Five & a half years ago my spouse came out to me as transgender. I didn't fully understand what that meant, but I have learned a lot since. She has told me what it was like growing up knowing she was different, but not being able to tell a soul, not even her parents, for fear of how they would react. Because at that time, being gay could mean being turned out by your family and being shunned by everyone you knew. Being transgender was even worse - the only examples oftransgender people were on shows like Jerry Springer or as the dead prostitute on a cop show. She knew from the earliest ages, she needed to keep her being transgender a secret if she wanted to live a "normal" life.
My spouse is so much happier and healthier now. She can sleep at night. It's easier for her to get up in the morning knowing she doesn't have to pretend to be someone she is not. But also since she came out, I have seen and felt the anger and apprehension of watching multiple anti-transgender bills being proposed and passed in other states and the fear of having the same happen here. I've spent sleepless nights worrying if our marriage will be invalidated, if our child will be taken away, if my spouse will lose her job, her healthcare, her freedom if bills like this and all the others being proposed today pass.
I have met several transgender people and have listened to their struggles - the joy of finally living as themselves and the fear of what that might mean as far as their place in society. They live in daily fear of losing jobs, respect, or as this bill is proposing, their civil rights.
For twenty years this law has protected sexual orientation, which includes gender identity for all Mainers. How is removing gender identity as a protected class a benefit? In what way can this amendment be viewed as anything other than harmful to an already marginalized community? What is to be gained except to discriminate against a tiny portion of the population that is doing no harm to anyone else as the past twenty years have demonstrated?
I have akeady seen the harm discriminating against transgender people can do. I have an acquaintance who is an established professional that had a signed employment contract terminated just because the employer found out she was transgender. After a year of tremendous stress and legal expense, the contract was honored, but without the protections of this bill, she would have had no recourse and might well still be unemployed. How much experience and expertise will be lost if discrimination against transgender people is allowed? And if one group's rights are taken away, who is next? What is protecting the rest but the whims of public opmion? The rights of all humans are inalienable. Have transgender people in Maine lost their humanity or is this bill just to stop them from being treated as human? I beg this committee - do not give this amendment any consideration other than to deny it. Please, vote no on this bill and others like it, now and for always. I thank you for your time and consideration.

194217:
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary
Committee:
Thank you for the opportunity to address you. My name is Erica Rand and I live in
Portland. I am an educator, an athlete, and someone who studies and writes about gender issues in sports. I am here to speak against the bills under consideration
today.
As an educator, I witness every day the harm caused to young trans people when
they face bias and stigma based on their identities. Over the past months, as this bias has escalated nationally, so has the evidence of harm: fear of coming to class, trouble concentrating, trouble getting schoolwork done, and more. This bias is a broad educational and mental-health issue, not just a sports issue.
At the same time, there is a sports issue on the table, and here are some facts I can
share with you as an expert on gender issues in sports. 1) cisgender girl and women athletes are not fragile people who need protection, as the rhetoric about these bills
often suggests. 2) Trans people--just like non-trans people---come in many shapes
and sizes, shapes and sizes that might or might not help them, depending on the
sports they participate in. This simple fact often gets forgotten when people worry

about trans girls in sports. 3) Bodies themselves do not win competitions--for a
reminder, check out the scouting reports that weren't so enthusiastic about Tom
Brady--and success depends on a lot more than gender: ranging from physical characteristics like eyesight to innumerable advantages that money can buy. Kids with access to sports camps or extra coaching, to medical care or nutrition, to fancier equipment--or sometimes to equipment at all: all those kids have competitive advantages. You can't abolish competitive advantage by getting rid of trans people. 4. In case you are thinking, oh well, these bills will only diminish the education, health, and joy of a few transgender people---which I will trust you are not thinking because that itself is way too big a cost-please understand the following: As the history of sports regulation has shown time after time, these bills
will also harm lots of girls and women who aren't trans by opening the door to invasive scrutiny and testing. This puts at risk any girl who doesn't look like a proper girl---or who, quite simply, does really well in her sport (because too many
people believe that strength and athletic prowess are really a guy thing). Far from protecting cisgender girls, this legislation about sports and bathrooms threatens
them, too.
Thank you for the opportunity to share my perspective and I urge you to vote no on
these measures. It is urgent to act against them now.
194185:
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee: Thank you for the opportunity to address the Committee. My name is Rev.
Erika Hewitt. l live in Bath, and l'm speaking in opposition of the bills before the committee today.
Before being invited to serve my denomination in a national role, l sen/ed as a church pastor for twenty years--many of them here in Maine. l chose Maine as my permanent home 12 years ago in large part because of who we are as a people: how Maine's
fiercely independent people also choose to look out for their neighbors.
When we care for someone who needs it, it's not out of pity. We might help others out
of kindness, or because we can--and often because either someone once helped us, or we know that we might need a hand someday.
Our lives are connected and interdependent. That is, to me, both a moral platform
and a religious statement: we belong to one another.
l believe, too., that all of us--you, me, and even the people in this room with whom l
profoundly disagree--come into this world whole. Not broken; not in need of redemption; not needing to do anything to earn worth and dignity. Everyone is inherently whole, worthy, and loved by a Force beyond our understanding.
Since some people, by virtue of who they are, are pushed to the margins or otherwise put at risk, we whose social privilege places us at the center of belonging have a
responsibiliw to protect and care for the vulnerable; the marginalized; the disempowered.
ln our country, our communities, and even our churches, transgender people are being dehumanized in attempts to deny their inherent dignity and worth. Laws and
policies that make transgender people an "other"--and the bills you're considering
today---feed this dehumanization.
As a faith leader, I urge you to recognize your legislative choices as bearing moral
and ethical weight: Whose integrity is worthy of protecting? What values and principles are you communicating by saying No to bills whose intent is to harm and diminish? If an ethos of interdependence and mutual care is how we wish to live, as
the people of Maine, which choice communicates that obligation to look out for one
another?
I urge you to vote "Ought not to Pass" on these bills. Thank you for the opportunity to share my perspective with the Committee.
